The Longspine squirrelfish Holocentrus rufus attains a maximum recorded total length of 35 centimeters [Li = 35 centimeters], placing it among the larger members of its genus within the family Holocentridae. This ultimate size is achieved after several years of somatic growth, with individuals inhabiting shallow coral reef environments in the tropical western Atlantic and Caribbean. Mature adults are commonly observed taking shelter within crevices and under ledges during daylight hours, emerging at night to forage on benthic crustaceans and small fishes. The species exhibits a moderately robust body form, large eyes adapted for nocturnal vision, and the characteristic elongated dorsal spines that give the squirrelfishes their common name. Field measurements from a recent survey of reef fish populations in the Bahamas recorded several individuals approaching the maximum length, though most adults encountered were considerably smaller. This maximum length represents the largest size recorded during extensive sampling efforts across the species' range and serves as a useful benchmark for comparative studies of body size evolution within the Beryciformes.

In contrast to the ultimate size, the total length at puberty for Holocentrus rufus has been determined to be 13.5 centimeters [Lp = 13.5 centimeters], a value derived from histological examination of gonadal tissue in specimens collected across multiple reef sites. At this length, individuals begin vitellogenesis and spermiation onset, marking the transition from the juvenile stage to a reproductively viable organism. The onset of gonad maturation at this relatively modest size compared to the ultimate total length suggests that energy is allocated towards reproductive activity well before somatic growth has ceased, a pattern common among iteroparous coral-reef fishes that experience size-dependent predation risk. Juveniles grow rapidly through the sub-adult size range, and the attainment of 13.5 centimeters typically occurs within the first two to three years of life under favorable conditions. Field records indicate that the smallest gravid individuals encountered during spawning season consistently fall near this length threshold, confirming its biological relevance as a marker of sexual maturation.

The wet weight at birth for newly emerged prolarvae of Holocentrus rufus is approximately 0.0004 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0004 grams], reflecting the small size of the fertilised ovum which has an egg diameter of roughly 0.92 millimeters. This remarkably low initial mass places the species among those producing tiny, pelagic yolk-sac larvae that undergo a period of endogenous nutrition before the onset of exogenous feeding. Following chorion rupture at the hatching event, the yolk-dependent larva must absorb its yolk reserves and develop functional feeding structures within a very short window. The age at birth, defined here as the time from fertilisation to eclosion, is 3 days [ab = 3 days] when eggs are incubated at a temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], a thermal regime consistent with summer surface water temperatures across much of the species' Caribbean distribution. Embryonic development proceeds rapidly at this temperature, with cleavage-stage embryos progressing through blastula and gastrula stages within the first 24 hours after gamete fusion. The short incubation period typical of tropical holocentrids minimizes the vulnerability of demersal or adhesive eggs to benthic predators.

At a stable water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], batch-spawning females of Holocentrus rufus release multiple clutches over an extended breeding season, with a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 93 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 93 eggs per day]. This fecundity estimate, drawn from data on the congener Holocentrus adscensionis adjusted for body size differences, reflects the high reproductive potential of large individuals, which can reach an ultimate wet weight of 329 grams [Wwi = 329 grams]. Field observations confirm that larger, older females contribute disproportionately to total egg production, a common life-history pattern among iteroparous teleosts that continue growing after maturation. The wet weight at puberty, corresponding to the 13.5 centimeter length threshold, is approximately 21 grams [Wwp = approximately 21 grams], a mass at which first spawning events become possible.

Maximum lifespan estimates for Holocentrus rufus in the wild, based on mark-recapture studies and otolith age validation, indicate that individuals can live for 15 years [am = 15 years] when maintained at average reef temperatures near 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. This longevity, combined with repeated spawning events across multiple seasons, allows for substantial lifetime reproductive output that compensates for the high mortality rates experienced by the tiny pelagic larvae and early juveniles. The relatively extended lifespan compared to many other cryptobenthic reef fishes is consistent with the species' moderate body size and its occupation of predator-sheltered microhabitats that reduce adult mortality. Senescent individuals exhibit reduced condition factors and diminished gonadal output in their final years, though few individuals in wild populations survive to the maximum age due to predation and disease. Comparative analyses within the Beryciformes suggest that the Holocentridae as a family share relatively slow life histories, with deferred maturity and long reproductive lifespans that buffer against recruitment variability in the variable reef environment. These demographic traits have important implications for the species' resilience to fishing pressure and habitat degradation across its range.
